bibliography.title: The science and art of testing in ice hockey: a systematic review of twenty years of research.
bibliography.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living

methods.review_scope: Relevant full-text sections and acceleration/speed table reviewed; secondary systematic review.

findings.text: The review inventories 55 on-ice tests from 107 studies, predominantly male and older cohorts. In its acceleration/speed table one adolescent cohort has no significant height or body-mass effect on performance tests; this concerns performance, not distance per push.

limitations: Abstract/metadata reviewed for this seed; findings are not transcribed as full-text verified.
2026-10-11 update supersedes seed review scope for the findings above only; historical provenance retained.
Secondary review cannot establish a universal null anthropometric effect, a mass/BMI distance coefficient, or exhaustive absence of stride-length equations.
Bibliography is Bournival et al., Frontiers; Chiarlitti et al./Journal of Sports Science & Medicine attribution for this PMCID is incorrect. Historical study ID retained.
Adolescent table entry is Martini et al. 2022, DOI 10.3390/ijerph19158952 (86 males, 113 females), not a push-distance model.

provenance.review_scope: Relevant sections/table reviewed; PMC later returned CAPTCHA.

bibliography.title: Measurement of temporal and spatial parameters of ice hockey skating using a wearable system.

methods.sensors: Five IMUs at pelvis, both shanks and both skates; no wrist sensor.
methods.review_scope: Relevant full text reviewed; original criterion-comparison study.
methods.participant_description: Six male and four female comfortable skaters.
methods.description: Forward straight skating on 14 m synthetic ice at 0.88–2.63 m/s, at least 3 s rest before and after each trial.

findings.text: The best pelvis-based same-skate stride-length method reported relative error 2 ± 6% under restricted straight synthetic-ice trials with at least 3 s rest before and after. Skate IMUs supplied temporal events; authors recommend two skate IMUs and one pelvis IMU.

limitations: Abstract/metadata reviewed for this seed; findings are not transcribed as full-text verified.
2026-10-11 relevant full-text review supersedes seed scope for the findings above only; historical provenance retained.
No wrist watch/Garmin validation; pelvis accuracy cannot be transferred to detected wrist pushes.
Stride spans successive strikes of the same skate, not each detected wrist push; step length, glide length, sensor trajectory and app distance are different definitions.
No turning, longer-distance or high-speed validation; height and mass describe participants but no anthropometric regression is reported.
Khandan et al., not Wimmer et al.

bibliography.title: Ice hockey skating sprints: run to glide mechanics of high calibre male and female athletes

methods.review_scope: Abstract reviewed; full-text review incomplete. Institutional manuscript excerpts available but direct retrieval failed.
methods.description: High-calibre male and female ice-hockey players performing 30 m sprints; centre-of-mass/lower-body motion capture.

findings.text: Peak skating speed was associated with peak leg strength, and lower-body technique differed between high-calibre male and female groups performing 30 m ice-hockey sprints.

limitations: No wrist sensor validation or height/leg-length/body-mass/BMI regression for metres per push in the inspected abstract.
Sample size not confirmed in inspected abstract material; do not infer it.
2020 print and 2018 online publication are one study.

bibliography.title: Anthropometric determinants of skating sprint kinematics in bandy
bibliography.journal: Book of abstracts, 30th ECSS Annual Congress

methods.review_scope: Conference abstract reviewed via institutional author record; refereed poster, not journal full paper.
methods.sensors: Two skate IMUs and nine timing gates.
methods.description: Two 80 m skating sprints; leg-length/BMI partial correlations.

findings.text: Leg length had moderate positive partial correlations with glide time, glide length and step length (r=0.40–0.49, p<0.05), controlling for BMI. Controlling for leg length, BMI correlated positively only with maximum velocity attained during acceleration (r=0.40).

limitations: Indirect bandy association, not causation or an individual prediction equation for hockey/wrist pushes.
Height was descriptive; leg length was analysed. No body-mass coefficient or BMI length multiplier.
Muscle-mass explanation is not measured body composition.
Refereed conference abstract is not a peer-reviewed journal full paper; ResearchGate DOI is an unverified locator.

provenance.review_scope: Full conference abstract reviewed; DiVA marks Refereed.

bibliography.title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Linear Skating Sprint in Male and Female Bandy Players: Analysis of Acceleration and Maximal Speed Phase

methods.review_scope: Relevant full-text methods/results/discussion/limitations sections reviewed in indexed publisher rendering; full-paper review incomplete, conservatively abstract_only.
methods.participant_description: 111 male and 74 female elite or junior-elite bandy players.
methods.sensors: Bilateral skate IMUs and 10 m photocell splits.
methods.description: 80 m linear sprints; height, mass and leg length measured.

findings.text: Glide and step lengths correlated with skating velocity in acceleration and maximal-speed phases. The reported analysis provides no individual anthropometric equation for distance per push.

limitations: Indirect bandy transfer; heterogeneous senior/junior sample.
Body composition, physical capacity, joint kinematics and muscle activation were not measured.
Rendered Table 1 swaps male height/mass entries; methods/abstract give 1.80 ± 0.05 m and 76.4 ± 8.4 kg. Do not propagate the swapped values.
Abstract/conclusion and discussion disagree on sex differences in glide time; verify figures/PDF before using this result.
Direct publisher/PDF retrieval failed; no complete full-paper review.

bibliography.title: Physiological and Biomechanical Characteristics of Inline Speed Skating: A Systematic Scoping Review

methods.review_scope: Full text accessible; relevant abstract/methods/evidence tables reviewed, conservatively abstract_only rather than complete full-paper review.
methods.description: Secondary synthesis; five biomechanics studies, three combined biomechanics/physiology studies.

findings.text: Of 22 included studies, five concerned biomechanics and three combined biomechanics and physiology; 59% had overall unclear risk of bias. Limited biomechanics evidence calls for assessments across skating skills and straight and curved tracks.

limitations: Secondary synthesis, not an original anthropometric validation study. Inline speed skating is not inline hockey.
Heterogeneous populations/methods; some biomechanics samples contain only one to five skaters.
Does not validate a height/weight-to-push-distance conversion or Garmin wrist accuracy.
No equation in inspected evidence tables is not proof of universal absence.
